title: Returning to the source
hookLine: renewers kept returning to the Qur'an and sunnah

lines: A MUDDY RIVER THROUGH A TOWN.
cards: A river runs through a town, and by the market it has picked up soil from the fields, leaves, whatever the streets wash into it. Want to know what the water was like at the start?

Study it where it runs past you, or walk upstream, past the fields, into the hills, to the spring where it comes out of the rock. This path has met many reformers this year, in very different places and times.
Look closely, and they keep walking upstream. Today: returning to the source.

teach.h: REFER IT TO ALLAH AND THE MESSENGER.
teach.b: First, the instruction is in the Qur'an itself. When believers disagree, in Pickthall's translation: "and if ye have a dispute concerning any matter, refer it to Allah and the messenger".
In practice, for Muslims, that means the Qur'an and the sunnah, the example of the Prophet, peace be upon him. Second, the Prophet framed it the same way.

teach.h: THE BOOK AND THE SUNNAH: TWO THINGS LEFT.
teach.b: In the Muwatta of Imam Malik, he is reported to have said he left two things, and as long as people hold to them they won't go astray: the Book of God and his sunnah. Third, the history.

We've met a hadith promising a renewer for the community at the head of every hundred years, and the people later generations called renewers. Al-Ghazali named a work the Revival of the Religious Sciences.
Shah Wali Allah of Delhi put the Qur'an into Persian so ordinary readers could reach it themselves. The reformers of Cairo urged Muslims to read the text again with open minds.
Different centuries, different lands, the same direction: upstream. Fourth, an honest note.

teach.h: THEY DISAGREED AT THE SPRING, TOO.
teach.b: Renewers didn't agree on what they found at the spring. Some stressed the law, some the inner life, some education, some politics, and they argued, sometimes bitterly.
Many scholars hold that the schools of law and the long chain of teachers are how a believer reaches the spring safely, not silt in the river; others called for reading the sources more directly.
Returning to the source didn't end the disagreement. It gave everyone the same place to stand while they had it.

how: Muslims turn to the Qur'an and the sunnah as the final reference in matters of faith and practice, read through scholars and the schools of law that interpret them, and some read a portion of the Qur'an daily.

games.q: your community is split over a question, and each side quotes its favorite teacher. what does Qur'an 4:59 point to?
o: refer it to Allah and the messenger: the Qur'an and the sunnah.
games.why: the verse says to refer a dispute to Allah and the messenger, and that's where renewers kept returning.

practice: Open a Qur'an, in Arabic or in translation, anywhere or at the beginning, and read slowly, a line at a time, as if no one had ever explained it to you; don't hunt for meaning yet.
If you don't have one with you, say the opening surah to yourself, or just its first line, in the name of Allah, the Beneficent, the Merciful, and listen to it as if for the first time.

wordCard.voice: Returning to the source. Renewal in Islam keeps going back to the Qur'an and the sunnah, upstream to the spring. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: back to the source. When things get muddy, the text itself comes before anyone's summary of it. Until tomorrow.
